nakta
(‘vow connected with night’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu scriptures—especially the धर्मशास्त्रस् and the purāṇas—insist that able-bodied persons must observe ड़स्तिन्ग् on एकादशी days (eleventh day after the full-मोओन् and the new-मोओन्). For the sake of those who cannot fast completely, eating once in a day is permitted. This is of two types: एकभक्त and नक्त.
In the former, one has to take his ड़ोओद् in day-time, a little after noon. In the latter, it is 6 to 3 ghaṭikās (one ghaṭikā = 24 minutes) after sunset.
In observing नक्त as a vrata (religious vow), one should take a small quantity of haviṣyānna (plain boiled ड़ोओद् without condiments and salt) after bath, sleep on the ground and observe moral virtues like truth very strictly.
See also EKABHAKTA and EKĀDAŚĪ.

Nakula
------------------------------------------
Nakula and सहदेव were the twins born to queen Mādrī (second wife of पाण्डु) by the grace of the twin deities, the अश्विन्स्.
Nakula, considered as the fourth of the Pāṇḍava brothers, was extremely handsome. He was an expert in the art of training and management of horses. Reṇumati was his wife and Niramitra his son from her. Śatānīka was his son born to द्रौपदी, the common wife of the five Pāṇḍavas.
Before युधिष्ठिर began the राजसूय sacrifice, नकुल was the first to start on the victory mission to collect enough wealth for the same.
During the ajñātavāsa (living incognito for one year) at Virāṭanagarī (capital of the king विराट) he had assumed the name Dāmagranthi and was taking care of the royal horses and the stable.
In the कुरुक्षेत्र war, he defeated शकुनि on the 14th day and दुर्योधन on the 15th day. But he was defeated by कर्ण, the next day.
During the महाप्रस्थान (final journey to हेअवेन्) he was the third to fall dead, the reason—according to युधिष्ठिर —being his pride about his handsome appearance.

nakṣatra
(‘star’, ‘constellation’)
------------------------------------------
In Hindu अस्त्रोनोम्य् and अस्त्रोलोग्य् नक्षत्र is an important subject. It (the lunar mansion) is the name of 1/27th part of the path of the मोओन् round the earth (13.33 degrees of the sky). The period of sidereal revolution of the मोओन् is a little less than 27 days and 8 hours. Thus the मोओन् travels through a little less than one नक्षत्र (cluster of स्तर्स्) every day. The day itself can be named after the नक्षत्र occupied by the मोओन् on that day. This system of naming seems to be very ancient since there are references to it even in the वेदस् (vide Ṛgveda 10.85.13).
The Atharvaveda (14.7) and the Maitrāyaṇīya Saṁhitā (2.13.20) give the names of 28 nakṣatras beginning with कृत्तिका and in this list is mentioned अभिजित् also which disappears from the lists of later periods.
The पुराणस् consider the 27 nakṣatras as the daughters of दक्ष and married to चन्द्र (Moon).
The nakṣatras are: अश्विनी, भरणी, कृत्तिका, रोहिणी, Mṛgaśiras, आर्द्रा, पुनर्वसु, पुष्य, Āśleṣa, Maghā, Pūrvaphālgunī, Uttaraphālgunī, Hastā, Citrā, Svātī, Viśākhā, अनूराधा, ज्येष्ठा, Mūlā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣa, Pūrva-bhādrapadā, Uttara-bhādrapadā, Revatī.
These nakṣatras are related to the rāśis (the twelve ज़ोदिअचल् सिग्न्स्).
Astrological works classify the nakṣatras as male and female and also as पुण्य (beneficent) and पाप (malefic).
In naming a new-born babe, the नक्षत्र in which it was born, is taken into consideration.
See also RĀŚI.
